title: Decision-Making Traps. Why Do We So Easily Set Aside What We Already Know?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Galef, Julia, The Scout Mindset: Why Some People See Things Clearly and Others Don’t, Portfolio 2021
Grove, Andrew S., Only the Paranoid Survive: How to Exploit the Crisis Points That Challenge Every Company, Currency Doubleday 1996
Heath, Chip; Heath, Dan, Decisive: How to Make Better Choices in Life and Work, Crown Business 2013
Kray, Laura J.; Gonzalez, Richard, Differential Weighting in Choice versus Advice: I’ll Do This, You Do That, “Journal of Behavioral Decision Making” 12 (1999)
Levitt, Steven D., Heads or Tails: The Impact of a Coin Toss on Major Life Decisions and Subsequent Happiness, “The Review of Economic Studies” 88 (2021)
Packer, J. I.; Nystrom, Carolyn, God’s Will: Finding Guidance for Everyday Decisions, Baker Books 2012

paragraphs: In the mid-1980s the American tech giant Intel began losing money on memory chips, the product it had started with and which was its pride. The management deliberated for almost a year, until Andrew Grove, one of the company’s leaders, asked its co-founder what a new chief executive would do if the board removed them both from their posts. The answer came at once: he would take the company out of the memory business. Following this sober conclusion, they made a radical decision and concentrated their efforts on developing processors. They had known the solution long before; what they lacked was the right vantage point from which to see it.

Most of us know dilemmas like this: a degree course that stopped being enjoyable long ago, or a flat that eats up half your salary. From the inside everything looks complicated, while from another person’s point of view it often turns out to be much simpler. Steven Levitt, a well-known economist, offered thousands of people who could not make up their minds the chance to use a virtual coin toss. Six months later it turned out that, with difficult decisions, those whom chance told to take the risk and who went ahead with a change were clearly happier than those who stayed with the old arrangement. For putting things off is also a decision; it is just that circumstances make it for us.

In the Gospel of Luke, crowds follow Jesus, moved by His teaching and a little carried away by the moment. Jesus turns to them and asks: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?” (Luke 14:28). Then He speaks of a king who, with ten thousand soldiers against twenty thousand, also first sits down to weigh his chances. If the calculation comes out badly, the king sends a delegation and asks for peace while the enemy is still far off. Honest counting, then, sometimes reveals a third way, something other than just “yes” or “no”.

This call comes from One who had Himself made the irrevocable decision to go to Jerusalem, though He knew what awaited Him there. Jesus does not want disciples won by momentum, so He invites people to sit down and count the cost, and He hides nothing as He does so. Prayer over an important decision is also a way of sitting down to think. It does not replace thinking. But you then do your calculations in the presence of the One who sees further than you do and for whom your worth does not depend on whether your choice turns out right.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: What decision are circumstances making for me because I avoid stopping to count the cost?
challenge: Before you put down your phone or close your computer today, think of one decision you have been putting off for more than a month. Put it into one simple question and ask God that question, exactly in the form in which it took shape in your mind.

paragraphs: In the mid-1980s the American technology pioneer Intel began to see shrinking profits from the sale of memory chips, the product that was the foundation of the company and had built its market position for years. Japanese competitors were supplying comparable components more cheaply and at better quality. Meanwhile, the management spent nearly a year in fruitless debate about how to solve the problem. Some pushed the idea of building a huge new factory, while others looked for salvation in niche segments of the market. But no one had the courage to propose radical cuts out loud. Memory chips were the company’s identity and had been a source of pride from the very beginning.

In mid-1985 Andrew Grove, then the number two at Intel, was sitting in an office with Gordon Moore, the company’s co-founder and chief executive. Both were worn out by months of fruitless discussion. Outside the window, in the distance, the Ferris wheel of a nearby amusement park turned lazily. It was against this backdrop that Grove asked the key question, which he later recounted in his memoirs: what would a new chief executive do if the board got rid of them both and brought in someone from outside? Moore answered without hesitation that such a person would take the company out of memory chips. Hearing that, Grove said plainly: “Why shouldn’t we walk out the door, come back in, and just do it ourselves?”

Intel began to withdraw from the memory market and bet on making processors, which soon came to dominate the global personal computer market. Yet the most fascinating thing in this whole story is something else. Two very intelligent men had a ready solution within arm’s reach. To see it, however, they needed a completely new perspective.
**Why do we so easily put off decisions whose outcome, deep in our hearts, we already know?**

sections.heading: A Change of Perspective
paragraphs: The question about a new chief executive works because for a moment it puts a person in a different chair. A new boss did not build this division, did not hire these people and does not have to defend decisions made ten years ago, so he simply sees what is there. Grove and Moore had all the data they needed much earlier, since they had known about the losses for a long time. Yet all it took was a change of perspective in their minds, and the right answer immediately became obvious to them.

Simply changing whose decision it is works in a similar way. In one psychological study, students were offered a choice between two career paths. The first was prestigious and well paid, though interest in it came mainly from pressure from parents and friends. The second offered more modest earnings but matched their real passions and plans. What happened? People advising someone else pointed to the second option clearly more often than those making the choice for themselves. We see someone else’s situation more sharply, because it is not weighed down by our own fear or by worry about what others will say.

Each of us has things we hold on to mainly out of habit, even though they stopped bringing any benefit long ago. It might be a degree course that stopped being enjoyable in the second year, or a flat that swallows half your salary. Sometimes it is a project into which so much time and money has gone that it is simply embarrassing to shut it down. From the inside each of these situations seems extremely complicated, while from a stranger’s point of view it often turns out to be surprisingly simple.

So when you are looking for an answer, it is worth turning the perspective around. Someone considering a job in another city should imagine that they have already taken it. Would they then want to go back to the old place and the old work? If the answer is no, then what keeps them where they are is fear of change rather than the real value of their present situation.

Thought experiments of this kind do not, of course, settle anything automatically; the final choice always belongs to the person. But they make it possible to gain priceless clarity. Their sole purpose is to separate what is truly valuable from what is merely familiar.

sections.heading: The Coin That Nudged People Toward Change
paragraphs: In January 2013 Steven Levitt, an economist at the University of Chicago, launched a website as an experiment for people who could not make a decision. The rules were simple: the participant described their dilemma, and the system tossed a virtual coin for them. One side meant change, the other staying with the status quo. The study covered both trivial matters, such as going on a diet, and fundamental choices, including quitting a job or ending a long-term relationship. Within a year users made more than twenty thousand tosses.

After two and after six months the researcher contacted the participants to find out what steps they had taken and how things had turned out for them. It turned out that many of them had indeed followed the coin, including on serious decisions. The key finding concerned precisely the weightiest dilemmas. Those whom the system pointed toward change felt clearly happier six months later, and more satisfied with their choice, than those who stayed with the old status quo. People who had opted for a revolution were also much more likely to say they would make the same decision again without hesitation.

These results must, however, be interpreted with caution. The participants signed up for the project themselves, so they are not a representative sample of society, and happiness was measured solely on the basis of their own subjective reports. Levitt writes openly about these limitations, and it is hard to draw from his analysis the conclusion that we should thoughtlessly leave every job we have doubts about. But there is another lesson in it, and a very interesting one. People who spend weeks pondering a change and cannot take the final step are being overly cautious. This happens because what we already know has a huge advantage in our minds, an advantage it has not objectively earned at all.

There was one more pattern hidden in the data. The coin gave an impulse to act only during the first two months. Decisions made after that were no longer related to the result of the toss: the initial nudge simply faded, and participants went back to their old pace.
Putting things off is also a decision. It is just that circumstances make it for us, and they rarely ask our opinion.

sections.heading: First Sit Down and Count
paragraphs: Jesus raises the subject of decisions in a context where few would expect it. In the Gospel of Luke, crowds follow Him, moved and probably a little carried away by the moment. But He turns to them and, instead of fanning their enthusiasm, sets hard conditions. Anyone who wants to be His disciple must be ready to put Him above their own family and to carry their cross, that is, to follow Him even when it comes at enormous cost (Luke 14:25–27).

Then Jesus tells two short stories. The first concerns a man who intends to build a tower, perhaps a watchtower by a vineyard, of the kind commonly built in the land of Israel at the time. He asks His listeners: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?” (Luke 14:28). Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to finish, everyone watching will start to ridicule him (Luke 14:29–30).

The verb used here, translated “count”, comes in Greek from a word meaning a small stone: it was with pebbles like these that accounts were kept in the ancient world. Jesus’ listeners could easily picture someone sitting in front of a pile of pebbles, moving them from place to place as he reckoned the cost of bricks, lime and workers, and the days needed to complete the project.

The second story is about a king who has ten thousand soldiers in his ranks, while an army of twenty thousand warriors is marching against him (Luke 14:31). He, too, first sits down and considers the situation before setting out for the battlefield. Both stories share the same motif: radical action must be preceded by stopping and calm calculation.

It is easy, though, to overlook the ending of this story. If the reckoning comes out unfavorably, the king, while the enemy is still far off, sends a delegation and asks for peace (Luke 14:32). An honest assessment, then, need not end in a simple choice between “yes” and “no”. Sometimes it reveals an entirely new, third way that no one had considered at the start.

It also matters a great deal whose lips these words come from. A few chapters earlier Luke noted that Jesus “resolutely set out for Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). He knew perfectly well what awaited Him, and yet from that moment His whole journey leads in that very direction. So the One speaking about counting the cost had counted it Himself beforehand and did not turn back from the path He had chosen.

Yet there is a tension in this text that should not be resolved too quickly. Jesus first calls for a well-considered decision, then adds that a true disciple gives up everything he has (Luke 14:33). Here an honest reckoning leads to a surprising conclusion, because it turns out that this decision requires the commitment of one’s whole life. But whoever has sat down and counted the cost is far more aware of their own choice than someone who has simply been swept along by the crowd.

sections.heading: The God Who Wants to Count with You
paragraphs: This scene tells us something important about God. Jesus does not want disciples won by momentum, so He invites you to sit down and count the cost, and He hides nothing as He does so. Faith in Luke’s Gospel resembles the decision of a person who, intending to put up a building, has counted the expenses and knows what he is choosing. Thinking is welcome in it.

This scene also tells you something important about yourself. A good decision has its own rhythm: first comes stopping and an honest calculation, including from a stranger’s point of view, and then action, without endlessly going back to options already rejected. Most of us mix up these stages: we can spend weeks analyzing which phone to buy, while in matters of fundamental importance we follow the crowd or our habits.

A simple distinction helps here. Some decisions can be reversed, such as trying a new recipe for dinner or signing up for a trial language course. Such matters are best settled quickly, because a mistake costs little, while hesitation eats up time and peace of mind. Other decisions bind us for years, such as marriage, a thirty-year mortgage, choosing a profession or moving with the children to the other end of the country. For these you need to sit down for a long time and count carefully, even if everyone around you is growing impatient.

One more thing helps: you do not have to weigh an important decision alone. The book of Proverbs puts it briefly: “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22). Prayer over an important decision is also a way of sitting down to count together. It does not replace thinking, because God usually guides people precisely through calm weighing of the arguments, the counsel of wise people and the time given to a matter for reflection. So you go on counting, but in the presence of Someone who sees further than you do and for whom your worth does not depend on whether your choice turns out right.

The same book adds a sentence that takes a good deal of fear out of decision-making: “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). Your part is to weigh the matter honestly; His part is to lead you on, even when your choice turns out to be wrong. If, after careful calculation, you still make a mistake, you will not fall out of His hand. A king who asks for peace hardly looks heroic, and yet his decision springs from an honest assessment of his strength.

questions: What decision are circumstances making for me because I avoid stopping to count the cost?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Think of one decision you have been putting off for more than a month. Put it into one simple question and ask God that question, exactly in the form in which it took shape in your mind.

**In action.** Take a sheet of paper and write the problem you are facing at the very top. Below it, answer in writing: what would a stranger do about this if they took over your life tomorrow? Then add a third possibility, something other than “yes” or “no”. Finally, write down the date by which you will make your final decision, and one small step you will take today. It might be a phone call, an email asking for details, checking a price, or arranging a conversation with someone who knows the subject. Take that step before you go to bed, and put the sheet away somewhere you will look on the date you set.
